---
title: "Part 2 – The claim, its estimand and its causal graph"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/cohabitation-one-day.html#/part-2-the-claim-its-estimand-and-its-causal-graph){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 2 is the conceptual middle of the day. It reads the paper, sets out what the five Multi100 analysts did with its claim, and argues that analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions. It then gives you two tools for saying which question you are answering, the estimand statement and the causal graph, and uses both on a feature of this claim that is easy to miss: every woman in the data cohabited, and who cohabits changed between the two periods, so the comparison is made within a group that the period itself helped to select.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, Part 2 | The paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the data and the unions of the two cohorts, the life table, the model on person-months and its result, the main finding by education, and the claim as SCORE selected it, with the hedge that the cut removes and the coefficient from a model with an interaction that Multi100 attached to it. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the five analysts | A table of what each of the five Multi100 analysts compared and reported, and the three conclusions that they reached from one file. Why they disagree is the question that Task 3 answers. | 6 minutes |
| Slides, the estimands run | Two studies set beside our five: the red-card estimates again as a single row, the four estimands that the twenty-nine teams were in fact pursuing, and the spread that collapses once the estimand is fixed. Then what under-specified research questions mean for the reading of many-analysts studies, and the steps from a theoretical to an empirical estimand that Lundberg and colleagues set out. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, the causal-graph crash course | Confounders, mediators and colliders; the causal stories that can lie behind one correlation; open and closed paths; total against direct effects; selection and feedback. | 14 minutes |
| Slides, the claim | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; who cohabits in each cohort; the causal graph of the claim; selection into cohabitation as conditioning on a collider; and the two readings of "cohabitors" that the adjustment sets of the menu answer. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the R tutorial | Optional, if the class wants it: R in one slide, reading and inspecting the union file, the verbs that work on rows and columns, one row per month, model formulas for the logit, the complementary log-log and the multinomial logit, a plot of the life table, causal graphs in R, and the error messages that you are most likely to meet. | 8 minutes |
| Task 2 in your report or working script, or [Browser lab](../../cases/cohabitation/lab.qmd#task-2-data) Task 2, with [Causal graphs and adjustment sets](../../companion/dags.qmd) as the slower companion | Count the unions of each survey and the 929 and 1,142 unions of the paper with their outcomes; compute the weighted shares of Hispanic, Black and white women among the cohabitors of each cohort; turn the unions into person-months with `spec_frame(unions)` and draw the life table. Write the [estimand statement](../../cases/cohabitation/lab.qmd#task-2-estimand-and-graph) with every bracket filled, saying which cohorts and what you hold constant. Then open `R/dag_starter.R`, take the `#` off the arrow from the period to marriage if you believe it, run `adjustmentSets(dag)`, `paths(dag, Z = "cohabits")` and `paths(dag, Z = c("cohabits", "education", "race"))`, and add the arrow from the period to the age at the start. Finish with two sentences: what keeping only cohabitors does to the comparison of the two periods, and which adjustment set answers which reading of "cohabitors". | 18 minutes |

**By the end of the part** you have the estimand behind the claim written in one sentence, a graph that includes only the arrows you are willing to defend, and two sentences on what the selection into cohabitation does to the comparison and on the adjustment that answers the reading of the claim that you hold.
